newsitem.title: USA: Kasich calls Clinton's attack a 'cheap shot'.
newsitem.headline: Kasich calls Clinton's attack a 'cheap shot'.

text.p: Republican Representative John Kasich on Sunday described as a "cheap shot" President Clinton's criticism of Congress taking an 11-day break without passing disaster aid for 33 states.
Clinton called Congress's decision to recess until June 3 without acting on legislation that would provide up to $8.4 billion in financial aid to victims of natural disasters "unconscionable."

In his weekly radio address to the nation Saturday, Clinton said: "Disaster doesn't take a holiday. In government, we must act because that is our duty as Americans. We cannot leave the victims without the help they need and deserve."

Kasich, chairman of the House Budget Committee, said on Fox News Sunday that he was surprised by Clinton's attack on Congress, and suggested it was unhelpful in the current climate of cooperation with the White House.

"I was a little bit taken aback by the president banging on the Congress like that," he said. "We have just had a couple of good weeks here of putting together tax relief for Americans and a balanced budget.
"If we are going to try to get things done let's try to keep the rhetoric down. I felt that was a cheap shot.
"I just think he shouldn't have done it and I don't understand it."
Kasich said he believed financial aid was already flowing to people in the disaster areas.
The decision to allow lawmakers to leave Washington without passing at least some interim relief for the victims has turned into a public relations nightmare for the Republican leadership.
With such a large number of states across the nation needing disaster relief, Democrats fumed over the failure to act -- as have many state and local officials of both parties.

While Republican congressional leaders insist that the Federal Emergency Management Agency still has $2 billion it can dispense, White House officials counter that a broad range of projects -- such as repairing damaged roads and bridges -- must wait until Congress returns.
Both parties support disaster aid, but Clinton has threatened to veto the $8.4 billion emergency measure because of unrelated spending and environmental amendments added by Republicans.
